p:AIA: Anguilla has no central bank of its own: it uses the EC dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, the monetary authority for eight places, Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and St Vincent and the Grenadines. The currency has been fixed at EC$2.70 to one US dollar since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling, backed by a legal requirement to hold reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation. One case is recorded. The Official Stanford Investors Committee sued the bank in Dallas in 2013 after it seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, alleging it fraudulently misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors. On 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, and did not rule on whether the allegations were true. For Anguilla the arrangement scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Governor Timothy Antoine, calling the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions. Gonsalves wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable, and that the spending invites disciplinary action; he proposed that the Monetary Council, which is made up of the member states' finance ministers, sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis, and said he had supported Antoine's appointment but wanted suitable and comfortable accommodation for him instead. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are made on and, by one report on the updated banknote family announced on 9 July 2026, prints them; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. The careers of the people who have run the bank are published, and they reach Anguilla through the union rather than through a central bank of its own. K Dwight Venner was Director of Finance and Planning in the Government of Saint Lucia from 1981 to 1989 and then governor from 1989 to 2015. Cecil Jacobs was appointed on transfer as Financial Secretary of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, having acted in that post in St Kitts from 1958 to 1961, and ran the institution from 1973 to 1989. Timothy Antoine had a 22-year career with the Government of Grenada, fourteen years of it as Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Finance, and advised the World Bank Group's executive director for Canada, Ireland and the Caribbean, before taking over as governor on 1 February 2016. p:BEN: Benin does not have its own central bank. Its money is the West African CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States, known by its French initials BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The franc is pegged, meaning held at a fixed rate, at one euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France guarantees, without condition or limit, to advance euros if the BCEAO's reserves run out. A cooperation agreement signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019 replaced the 1973 one and ended the requirement that the BCEAO keep at least half its reserves at the French Treasury, and France withdrew its representatives from the BCEAO board, its Monetary Policy Committee and the banking commission, though one independent committee member is still appointed in consultation with the French government. Benin scores 40 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, mainly from money-laundering risk in its banks and corruption in the country. One case is documented at the central bank: a summit of regional heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation in January 2011, after he was criticised for ignoring a 23 December decision by the union's finance ministers giving Alassane Ouattara power over the institution, and the account says the BCEAO paid out 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date. The bank's own statement said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders, and Dacoury-Tabley said afterwards that he agreed to hand it in because that is what was asked of him. Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs, or by another figure 300 billion, to Gbagbo after being dismissed; no audit result is reported, so that is unproven. The accounts are audited by firms appointed in pairs, one doing the work and one standing in: Deloitte Benin with Mazars Benin for Benin, and Deloitte Cote d'Ivoire with Mazars Senegal for the BCEAO itself. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The Banque de France's own director general of banknote manufacturing has called the BCEAO its largest export customer. The BCEAO's published accounts do not name the maker. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of the reserves is run by outside institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it has bought units in an investment fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and that it has joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program managed by the World Bank, worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. Together the two sets of fund units came to 344,611 million FCFA at the end of 2025, and the accounts group the BISIP K units with the holdings kept for immediate liquidity. The governors' careers are published, and they reach Benin through the union. Jean-Claude Kassi Brou joined the International Monetary Fund in 1982, worked as an economist and senior economist in several African countries, was the IMF's resident representative in Senegal from 1990 to 1991 and the World Bank's representative for Chad; he worked at the BCEAO from 2000 to 2008, was President of the ECOWAS Commission from 1 March 2018 to 3 July 2022, and became governor on 3 July 2022. Tiemoko Meyliet Kone joined the bank in 1975 and was its National Director and Alternate Governor at the IMF from 1991 to 1998, was chief of staff to Prime Minister Guillaume Soro from 2007 to 2010 and Minister of Construction, Urban Planning and Housing in 2010, was governor from 2011 to 2022, and has been Vice-President of Cote d'Ivoire since April 2022, appointed on 19 April 2022. The ministry he held was construction and housing, not finance. Moving between jobs is not wrongdoing.

p:AGO: The National Bank of Angola issues the kwanza (AOA). Angola scores 42 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is secrecy about who owns money and corruption (index score 32 of 100). Government pressure was reported in 29 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, nearly all pressing the bank to cut rates or ease, with 8 threats to replace leaders. On 14 August 2020 the Supreme Court convicted former governor Valter Filipe (eight years), BNA manager Samalia (five years), José Filomeno dos Santos (five years) and businessman Sebastião (six years) of embezzlement, fraud and influence peddling over an attempted transfer of $500 million to a London account, which a British bank blocked. The Constitutional Court is also named in the case. Goznak, the Russian state printer, printed the 5,000-kwanza note. KPMG audits the bank's accounts, and signed off on the 2021 accounts with one reservation and seven emphases, against three reservations and six emphases the year before. The London firm Gemcorp Capital held 56 percent of the bank's external assets at the end of 2023, 601,697 million kwanzas or about 725 million US dollars. For the 2019 and 2020 accounts Gemcorp did not say what it had invested the central bank's money in, so the bank had to carry the holding at nil, and it then renewed the investment for a further six years. Both facts come from the newspaper Expansao reading the bank's accounts rather than from the accounts themselves: the bank's own website publishes no documents a reader can open. On Friday 27 October 2017 President Joao Lourenco exonerated Valter Filipe as governor of the Banco Nacional de Angola and named Jose de Lima Massano in his place, returning Massano to the post he had held until January 2015 and taking him from the chairmanship of the executive board of Banco Angolano de Investimentos. A note from the President's Civil House says the exoneration was at Filipe's own request, and no other official reason is given; the exit came eleven days after the President criticised the bank in a speech on 16 October, and no connection between the two is reported. Massano's own career is on record: he was governor for close to ten years between 2010 and 2023, became a Senior Minister in the President's office in June 2023, and had earlier been chief executive of Banco BAI and an executive director of the state-owned BPC. His biography gives no dates for either bank, and whether BAI is privately owned is not stated. Moving between jobs is not wrongdoing.
p:ETH: The National Bank of Ethiopia issues the birr. It scores 34 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 65% of the 194 places scored. Its legal independence is low: 0.495 of 1 on one index of 42 rules and 0.291 of 1 on another, rank 176 of 191. Government pressure was reported in 3 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, mostly pressing to cut rates or ease. One case is recorded. In March 2008 Ethiopian anti-corruption officials arrested 26 people after 90 kilos of fake gold were found in the bank's vaults: 7 from the bank, 4 from the Ethiopian Geological Survey and 15 businessmen and collaborators. What is known covers the arrests only, not charges or court outcomes. Some of the notes are made abroad: the bank awarded Francois-Charles Oberthur Fiduciaire of France a 19.6 million birr share of a 206 million birr banknote printing deal, covering the 50 birr note. Mamo Mihretu was appointed governor in January 2023, in an announcement dated 20 January, replacing Yinager Dessie; at the time he was chief executive officer of the state-owned company Ethiopian Investment Holdings, and before that he had been a senior private sector specialist at the World Bank, a senior policy adviser to the Prime Minister and Ethiopia's chief trade negotiator. On 30 November 2023 the standing parliamentary committee for Planning, Budget and Finance Affairs questioned governor Mamo Mihretu for nearly four hours. Its chair, Desalegn Wodaje, called for renewed efforts against the parallel currency market and said the bank has to use all policy options including devaluation, if it is necessary to bridge the widening gap. That is a parliamentary committee telling the bank which policy to adopt, in public, rather than an inquiry into how the bank has behaved.
p:COD: The Central Bank of the Congo issues the country's money. In April 2021 a report by Congo's state finance inspectorate, the IGF, called a 43 million US dollar transfer from a central bank account at BGFI Bank to the food importer Egal an embezzlement of public funds, and said the bank kept false accounts to cover it: its 2013 accounts showed about 43.1 million dollars in that account when the real balance was about 119,000 dollars. The former governor Deogratias Mutombo, the bank and PricewaterhouseCoopers did not respond to the journalists who reported this from leaked BGFI documents. On 25 October 2023 the accounts of Mutombo and of Albert Yuma, former board chairman of the mining company Gecamines, were frozen over an alleged embezzlement of 25.521 million dollars, with both men required to remain available to the national audit court; that allegation is unproven and still under investigation. Belgium's federal prosecutor also opened a money laundering investigation into Mutombo and five others, with searches in September 2023; as of October 2024 the prosecutor said no suspect had been charged. The bank scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Giesecke+Devrient printed the 200-franc note issued on 31 July 2007. The bank's accounts are audited by Ernst & Young RDC of Kinshasa, which gave an unqualified opinion on the year ended 31 December 2024. In a communique that reached the state news agency ACP on Wednesday 23 September 2026 the Cour des comptes, Congo's audit court, announced an audit mission at the Banque Centrale du Congo to examine the bank's treasury operations for the 2025 financial year, as part of checking how the 2025 finance law was carried out. The court's First President, Jimmy Munganga, instructed the bank's services to hand the auditors the documents they need. No start or end date is given, and parliament's review of the 2025 accounts-settlement bill and of the 2027 finance bill waits on the court filing its report.
p:LSO: Lesotho issues the loti, and the South African rand circulates alongside it. Under the Common Monetary Area, which replaced a Rand Monetary Area agreement signed in December 1974 and was followed by a Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992 when Namibia joined, member currencies are pegged to the rand one for one and are legal tender only in the country that issues them; Lesotho must back what it issues fully with rand assets, and South Africa pays it an imputed return on rand circulating there. All five of its current notes, introduced on 23 December 2021, are printed by De La Rue. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared in the Ficksburg Magistrates Court on fraud and money laundering charges over 57 million rand said to have been stolen from the Central Bank of Lesotho. The Hawks, a South African police unit, said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa, and that some officials were already before court in Lesotho. The charges are unproven. Its 2023 accounts were audited by Moteane, Quashie & Associates with SizweNtsalubaGobodo Grant Thornton. Lesotho scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and corruption and secrecy around the bank is its weakest side, at 60. At a hearing on Monday 8 June 2026, at which the Auditor General presented consolidated financial statements for 31 March 2023 and 2024, the parliamentary Public Accounts Committee called for a forensic audit of the Central Bank of Lesotho to trace missing public money. Its chairperson, Machabana Lemphane-Letsie, said the bank must undergo a forensic audit and say who the money had been paid to. The figures in the report do not agree with each other: its headline puts the gap at M3.9 billion, while the statements it describes show government cash of M5.91 billion at 31 March 2024 against M2.82 billion in the consolidated accounts, a difference of M3.09 billion, which a quotation in the same piece also gives. The committee resolved that the Auditor General's office submit a budget for the audit by 30 June; that office said it has neither the expertise nor any budget allocated for one. The bank resisted, citing its own 2000 Act, which provides for an external auditor and limits the Auditor General to auditing currency balances rather than government payments the bank makes for the state.
p:MAR: Bank Al-Maghrib issues Morocco's dirham, held to a pre-announced peg, meaning a fixed rate, against the euro. It prints the notes and mints the coins at its own unit, Dar As-Sikkah, founded in 1987, and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Morocco scores 28 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported between 2010 and 2018. Two cases are on record, both under investigation and unproven. In 2022 the bank complained to the prosecutor's office about one of its own staff and a service provider over suspected corruption in awarding contracts, with no amounts, charges or ruling given. On 4 July 2019 it said 1.2 million dirhams, about 125,000 US dollars, had been stolen while cash was moved from the Dar As-Sikkah mint to northern cities, and opened an investigation, with no findings reported. Abdellatif Jouahri was named wali, or governor, in 2003, coming from the presidency of the CIMR, a private-sector employers' pension body. On 24 March 2023 Driss Sentissi, president of the Mouvement Populaire's parliamentary group, wrote to the presidency of the parliamentary commission on finance and economic development asking that wali Abdellatif Jouahri be summoned before parliament to explain the rise in the key rate from 2.5 per cent to 3 per cent. The Mouvement Populaire is an opposition party, and whether the commission agreed to summon him is not reported, so what is documented is the demand and not a decision of parliament.
p:MRT: The Central Bank of Mauritania issues Mauritania's money, the ouguiya, and scores 30 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. One case is recorded, from 2020 and 2021, and it is still an investigation. In July 2020 police working under the Nouakchott-Ouest prosecutor arrested six people, one of them a bank employee, over foreign currency taken from the central bank. Early reports put the amount at about 1 million US dollars and later reports at 2.4 million, plus 500,000 dollars in counterfeit notes. By March 2021 seven people were in pretrial detention, presumed to have taken about 1 million dollars, and supporters held a sit-in demanding a quick trial. No trial or verdict is reported. The governor also signed an agreement with the World Bank treasury for advice on managing reserves. Central Banking reported on 30 July 2004 that President Maaouiya Ould Taya had sacked the chairman of the Central Bank of Mauritania, the day after sacking his whole economic team, and that Zeine Ould Zeidane, formerly an adviser to the president, was installed in his place. The report names neither the sacked chairman nor any reason and gives no calendar date, saying only that it happened on the Monday. It rests on a single relayed account by IRIN, so it is a claim, not confirmed.
p:HRV: Croatia uses the euro, so the European Central Bank sets its monetary policy, for 21 countries in all; the ECB is also one of 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. The country's own central bank is the Croatian National Bank. In January 2022, after media reports, the Zagreb prosecution and the financial regulator HANFA opened inquiries into whether senior bank officials had traded securities of commercial banks they supervise on inside information. The bank said its executives sold shares before the ban took effect and that trading bonds was not prohibited; the inquiries remain open and nothing is proven. Two further cases concern the ECB: between 2016 and 2018 the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration over ECB president Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of bankers, and the ECB declined its recommendation that he give it up; and in 2015 a speech on asset purchases was published only the morning after a private London event, which the ECB called an internal procedure error. Ernst & Young d.o.o. audits the Croatian bank's accounts for 2025 to 2027. Croatia scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. On 4 October 2016 the Ministry of Finance asked the European Central Bank for an opinion on a draft act amending the Act on the Croatian National Bank, and the ECB replied on 28 October 2016 in Opinion CON/2016/52. The draft would have let the State Audit Office carry out an annual audit of the bank's business operations and made the bank's reports subject to a parliamentary adoption vote. The ECB said the parliamentary vote would affect the bank's institutional independence, and that the draft was unclear, contradictory and failed to satisfy the requirements and safeguards it set out.
p:BGR: Bulgaria's central bank is the Bulgarian National Bank. On 1 January 2026 the country swapped the lev for the euro at 1.95583 lev to the euro and joined the Eurosystem, the group of national central banks that works with the European Central Bank, so its governor now sits on the body that sets interest rates. Its own large case concerns Corporate Commercial Bank, Corpbank, which collapsed in June 2014: prosecutors charged two former deputy governors responsible for supervision with failing, from February 2010, to take the measures the law required against the bank, allegedly to benefit its shareholders. Gounev was charged in June 2014 and removed from office by court order that December, and Simeonov about ten months later; neither charge is proven, and the accusation that Corpbank's majority owner embezzled 206 million leva is likewise unproven. The state's Bulgarian National Audit Office checks the books under a continuing legal mandate, Oberthur Fiduciaire AD has handled banknote production since 2014, and Louisenthal supplied the thread, foil and watermark for the 100-lev note that became legal tender on 28 December 2018. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and belongs to the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which offers advice, training or asset management without the page saying which Bulgaria uses. About 60 per cent of its 41 tonnes of gold sits outside its own vaults, stored at the Bank of England, which stores the metal rather than managing it. Two findings sit at the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman found maladministration over President Mario Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum whose members include private bankers, and recommended in January 2018 that he suspend it, which the ECB declined; and a speech by Coeure to a private London event on 18 May 2015 about front-loading asset purchases was published only the following morning, which the ECB called an internal procedure error. Kalin Hristov, long a member of the Governing Council and deputy governor for the Issue Department, joined the supervisory board of the commercial DSK Bank in August 2025; no ethics finding is recorded. Bulgaria scores 30 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. On 5 March 2015 Parliament voted 84 to 0 to set up an ad hoc committee of inquiry into the collapse of Corporate Commercial Bank, to examine the conduct of the state bodies and institutions meant by law to exercise the control that should have prevented the bank being drained, over the years 2009 to 2014. The Bulgarian National Bank's banking supervision arm is named among those bodies.
p:MNE: The Central Bank of Montenegro does not issue money. Montenegro took the euro on its own: the Deutsche Mark became sole legal tender on 1 January 2001 and the euro replaced it in March 2002. The bank issues no euros and is not a member of the European System of Central Banks, but has a repo line, a short-term loan arrangement, of up to 250 million euros with the Eurosystem. It scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Three cases are documented, all alleged and unproven. In July 2018 the bank's Council reportedly found that deputy governor Irena Radovic put personal interest ahead of the public interest and disclosed business secrets, and the bank asked parliament to dismiss her; she called the decision illegal retaliation and said she would sue, and no court has ruled. The NGO MANS said five payments totalling 4,100 euros went to relatives of governor Radoje Zugic in 2017 and 2018; he reportedly said he did not act illegally. In July 2012 MANS alleged to a prosecutor that First Bank got a 44 million euro state loan in 2008 it could not repay; no charge has been brought. “Ernst&Young Montenegro” Ltd Podgorica audits the bank's accounts. Zugic has moved between the bank and the government several times: he was Deputy Director General for Payment System Operations at the bank from 2001 to 2004, director of Montenegro's Pension and Disability Insurance Fund from 2004 to 2010, Governor from 2010 to 2012, Minister of Finance from 2012 to 2016, Advisor to the Prime Minister from May to October 2016, and Governor again since October 2016; he also sat as a board member representing state capital at the commercial banks Podgoricka banka, before its privatisation, and Prva banka Crne Gore. In October 2022 Dejan Djurovic, a member of parliament for the Democratic Front, tabled amendments to the Central Bank of Montenegro Law that would have cut short the six-year mandates of vice-governor Zorica Kalezic and three members of the bank's Council. The bank said in writing that the proposal directly undermines the independence guaranteed to it, and the IMF's mission chief, Srikant Seshadri, said the Fund had told Parliament directly that the existing system should not change.
p:EST: Estonia uses the euro, so interest rates are set not by the Bank of Estonia but by the European Central Bank, for the 21 European Union countries that use the currency. The one Estonian case ended in acquittal: on 5 March 1999 the Tallinn City Court found Siim Kallas, a former head of the bank, and Kaju not guilty of abuse of power and of submitting false information over the loss of 10 million US dollars from the North Estonian Bank, a charge of preparing to embezzle having been dropped two weeks earlier; the prosecutor, Jaan Naaber, appealed ten days later. Two findings concern the European Central Bank. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration and recommended that President Mario Draghi give up his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and bank executives; the bank declined and he kept it. And on 18 May 2015 board member Benoît Cœuré told a private London event that the bank would front-load its asset purchases, the speech appearing only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error. Six career moves between that bank and private finance are recorded, among them Jorg Asmussen going to the bank Lazard; a job move is not an accusation. The Estonian bank's other ties are to the auditors Ernst & Young Baltic AS and Forvis Mazars and the fund manager BlackRock. It scores 19 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. At the end of September 2017 five members of the Riigikogu, from the EKRE, Vabaerakond and Keskerakond groups, initiated a bill to compensate holders of VEB Fund certificates out of Eesti Pank's profit distributions, under which parliament would direct 50 per cent of the bank's annual distribution, 10 to 15 million euros, to the certificate holders. Eesti Pank replied that its own council decides how its profit is distributed.
p:KWT: The Central Bank of Kuwait issues the Kuwaiti dinar and holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar announced in advance. Its assets were 36.4 billion US dollars at the end of 2025, and it is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Two accounting firms check its books, Al-Aiban, Al-Osaimi & Partners of Ernst & Young and KPMG, Safi Al-Mutawa & Partners, which signed off the accounts for the fiscal year ended 31 March 2013, and Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank. One case is recorded and it is unproven: the Kuwaiti newspaper Al Jarida, citing unnamed sources, reported that the securities regulator had decided to refer Governor Mohammad Al Hashel to prosecutors over a suspected breach of investment rules involving shares in a local bank. He denied it, saying he had never traded shares in a listed company while in senior posts; the regulator did not answer Reuters' calls. Governor Basel Al-Haroon, in post since April 2022, worked at the bank from 1989 to 2006 and from late 2006 to 2012, and in between and afterwards led a Kuwaiti investment company and was vice chairman of a Kuwaiti bank from 2016 to 2018. No ethics finding is recorded. Kuwait scores 34 of 100, and 3 of 15 on how much it tells the public. The law the bank runs under lets the executive direct it, and this is a standing arrangement with no end date rather than an episode. Article 38 of Law No. 32 of 1968, as the Central Bank of Kuwait publishes it in English, provides that the Minister of Finance may issue directives to the bank and that such directives become binding on it, with a decision of the Council of Ministers final.
p:HKG: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority runs the Hong Kong dollar as a currency board, meaning it is tied to another currency: the monetary base is fully backed by US dollar assets in the Exchange Fund. The link began on 17 October 1983 at 7.80 Hong Kong dollars per US dollar, and since May 2005 the authority sells Hong Kong dollars at 7.75 and buys at 7.85. It scores 35 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case is recorded: in 2012 a Legislative Council subcommittee found that former chief Joseph Yam Chi-kwong should bear “ultimate responsibility” for investors' losses on Lehman's minibonds. The authority replied that the report had not fully taken into account the information it submitted, and some members prepared a minority report. One career move is recorded, and it is his: Joseph Yam headed the Office of the Exchange Fund from 1991 to 1993 and ran the authority from 1 April 1993 to 30 September 2009, and after leaving he was an independent non-executive director of China Construction Bank from 2010 until 23 October 2013, was elected in April 2011 to the board of the Swiss bank UBS AG, where he sat on its risk committee and its corporate culture and responsibility committee from 2011, and sat on the UBS Group AG board from November 2014 to May 2017. Banknotes are printed in Hong Kong by Hong Kong Note Printing Limited, in which the government keeps management control and a majority stake. The authority's relationship to the government is its founding design rather than something later taken from an independent bank, and it is a standing arrangement with no end date. The HKMA's own annual report describes how the Legislative Council passed amendments to the Exchange Fund Ordinance in 1992 empowering the Financial Secretary to appoint a Monetary Authority, and the HKMA began work on 1 April 1993. The Monetary Authority is appointed to assist the Financial Secretary, the Exchange Fund is under his control, and the powers are exercised by his delegation.
p:SWZ: The Central Bank of Eswatini, set up in 1974, issues the country's currency, fixed at par to the South African rand under the Common Monetary Area. One licensing fight runs through two findings. In 2017 the bank's evaluations team recommended rejecting Farmers Bank's application for a commercial banking licence, warning it would tarnish the integrity of the bank's licensing policy, and it was turned down late that year. Governor Majozi Sithole said a royal command required him to attend a meeting about the venture on 14 July 2017, and in May 2018 finance minister Martin Dlamini told the bank that King Mswati III had ordered an investigation into its reluctance to license it. A conditional licence followed in September 2018 after a royal command. The bank revoked it on 5 October 2020 because the source of the seed capital was unexplained; an appeal chaired by commerce minister Manqoba Khumalo ruled in December 2020 that the licence should stand, and the bank reinstated it in January 2021 while objecting to procedural improprieties. A 2022 forensic report by Kroll, commissioned by the bank, said parties outside the bank had likely intervened and instructed it to proceed, and that 89 million rand of seed capital had gone from 2019 into silver bullion the bank could not verify existed. That finance minister had run the bank himself: Martin Dlamini was its Governor from July 1997 to November 2013, having worked there for 30 years in all, and was Minister of Finance from November 2013 to November 2018, which is the one career move documented here and names no commercial employer. In October 2023 the bank moved its portfolio of special drawing rights to Crown Agents Investment Management, which manages it and trains bank staff; Giesecke+Devrient of Germany printed the new 20 lilangeni note. Eswatini scores 36 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its written independence is 0.373 of 1 on the Cukierman method, where 1 means the bank holds the power. The bank's accounts are audited by SNG Grant Thornton Chartered Accountants (Eswatini) of Mbabane, which signed its report on the statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 on 26 August 2026. The state's own side of that licensing fight is documented too. Governor Majozi Sithole said a royal command required him to attend a meeting about the venture on 14 July 2017, and in May 2018 finance minister Martin Dlamini told the bank that King Mswati III had ordered an investigation into its reluctance to license Farmers Bank. A conditional licence followed in September 2018 after a royal command, and when the bank revoked it the appeal that overrode the revocation was chaired by a minister. What the officials were accused of stays with the two cases above; what the state did was to order an investigation into the bank's own supervisory decision and then override it.
p:BIH: The convertible mark is issued by the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina under a currency board: marks are put into circulation only against convertible foreign currency the bank holds, at 1.95583 marks to the euro, and its monetary liabilities may never exceed its foreign currency assets. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and it has joined the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which offers advice, training and asset management, with the announcement stating the membership rather than which of those services the bank takes. Its law scores 0.899 of 1 for independence, 11th of 155 countries, and no government pressure was reported in the quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is documented: in 2023 a criminal complaint accused governor Senad Softic of suspected wrongdoing in several matters, including a project to acquire an office building in Pale and a procedure to buy land in Sarajevo. The prosecutor's office said in February 2023 that it had opened a case and was verifying the allegations, which remain unproven, while the bank said examining allegations is not an investigation and that reports of one were untrue. Grant Thornton d.o.o. Banja Luka audited the 2016 accounts. The bank holds 3.5 tonnes of gold and scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One career move is recorded. The Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina's own profile page gives Jasmina Selimovic's dated career: at the Faculty of Economics in Sarajevo since 2004, its Dean from 2018 and renewed in 2022; in the Fiscal Council's advisory group from 2011 to 2015; an independent member of the Supervisory Board of Raiffeisen Bank Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2018; president of the board of the Sarajevo Canton Institute of Health Insurance since 2021; and a member of the bank's Governing Board from 3 January 2024. The central bank's page leaves the ownership of Raiffeisen Bank Bosnia and Herzegovina unstated; that bank's own ownership page lists Raiffeisen SEE Region Holding GmbH as sole owner at 100 per cent, with no state shareholder, which is what makes this a move involving a private bank. Moving between jobs is not wrongdoing.
p:SLE: The Bank of Sierra Leone issues the leone and scores 36 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption and secrecy, at 66. Under the 2019 Bank of Sierra Leone Act, sacking the governor needs a two-thirds majority in parliament. In August 2018 the recently elected president dismissed the governor, and Kelfala Kallon was appointed on 15 August as the bank's third governor in 17 months; neither the dismissed governor nor either side's reason is named. On 22 November 2021 Kallon told parliament that he had bribed people hoarding the leone to bring it back into the banking system. The Anti-Corruption Commission investigated and said in May 2022 that he had meant cash swap operations in which the bank sold about 68.6 million United States dollars of foreign currency in 2021, that the word was used in error, and that it had closed the investigation after advising him to choose his words more carefully. On 13 March 2023 President Julius Maada Bio sent Kallon on indefinite leave and named his deputy, Ibrahim Stevens, interim head; no official reason was given, Kallon did not respond, and the president was reported to be bypassing the 2019 Act. De La Rue printed the 10-leone note of the redenominated series introduced on 1 July 2022, and the West African Monetary Institute manages the Stabilization and Cooperation Fund, in which the bank holds 63.59 million new leone. One career is on file, and every outside employer in it is public or academic. The Bank of Sierra Leone's own board page gives names, roles and appointment dates and no employers at all, so this comes from a university biography: Ibrahim L. Stevens spent a decade at the Bank of England, including as Senior Adviser at its Centre for Central Banking Studies, was Director of Research at the Bank of Sierra Leone from 2008 to 2010 on secondment from the Bank of England, worked with the International Growth Centre at the London School of Economics and advised Rwanda's finance ministry on a project funded by GIZ, became Deputy Governor in July 2014 and was reappointed in 2019, became First Deputy Governor after the 2019 Act, and has been Governor since November 2023. Moving between jobs is not wrongdoing.
p:BLZ: The Central Bank of Belize issues the Belize dollar, held at a fixed rate to the US dollar. In August 2021 governor Gustavo Manuel Vasquez lost his post. Prime Minister John Briceno said the board had recommended he resign because of a lot of policy differences. Vasquez wrote that his appointment was terminated on the instructions of the Ministry of Finance, that he faced opposition from it, and that he had tried to restore the bank's integrity and operational autonomy. Castillo Sanchez & Burrell, LLP, Chartered Accountants audited the 2013 accounts, and De La Rue printed the new 100-dollar note introduced on 4 August 2025. Belize scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and it tells the public little, 4 of 15 on a transparency measure in 2019. One career move is recorded, out of the bank and back into it. The Central Bank of Belize's own Office of the Governor page gives Kareem Michael as Monetary Economist in 2000 and Deputy Director of Research in 2008, says he resigned in 2014 to become Senior Business Analyst at Belize Electricity Limited, and records him returning as Deputy Governor in November 2017, Acting Governor on 13 August 2021 and Governor on 1 December 2021. Who owns Belize Electricity Limited is not stated there, and it is a utility rather than a financial firm. Moving between jobs is not wrongdoing.
n:Magyar Nemzeti Bank domestic vaults, H: The Magyar Nemzeti Bank keeps Hungary's gold at home. Its own press release of October 2018 says the stock of gold reserves had already been transported to Hungary, and that the reserves were increased and moved in physical form in the first part of October 2018, taking the holding from 3.1 tons to 31.5 tons, a tenfold rise. Where in Hungary the gold is kept is not stated, so no particular vault or city is claimed here.
n:Banco de Mexico main vault, Mexico Cit: The Bank of Mexico keeps a small part of its gold in its own vault in Mexico City. Its December 2016 answer to a transparency-law request, as reported, puts 1.05 per cent of the gold in Mexico as at the end of October 2016, the rest being abroad. The bank gave no bar or coin count for the gold held at home, unlike the 7,265 bars it listed for the Bank of England. The figures in the article reporting the answer do not add up, which is why what rests on it is marked as a weak source.
